why: Working it from the definition gives a discontinuity at 0 as well — on the whole interval (-1,0) the function is identically 1 while f(0)=0 — so it is discontinuous at every integer except 1, which is option D, not the keyed option B.
The old solution started one counting route, abandoned it mid-sentence with 'Actually', started a second route, and then jumped to the printed figure without ever multiplying anything out.
solution:
Side I has 8 chairs and must contain the 4 particular men; side II has 8 chairs and must contain the 2 particular men. That leaves \(16-4-2=10\) unrestricted people, of whom \(8-4=4\) must go to side I and \(8-2=6\) to side II.

Step 1 — split the 10 unrestricted people. Choose which 4 of them sit on side I:
\(\binom{10}{4}=\dfrac{10\times 9\times 8\times 7}{4\times 3\times 2\times 1}=\dfrac{5040}{24}=210\) ways.
The remaining 6 go to side II, so no further choice is needed.

Step 2 — seat each side. Side I now has a fixed set of 8 people and 8 distinct chairs, giving \(8!\) arrangements; side II likewise gives \(8!\) arrangements.

Total \(=210\times 8!\times 8!\).

Hence (C).

why: The old solution wrote two broken half-finished fractions with trailing dots, then asserted the product equals s/(s-b) without deriving it.
solution:
From \(a-2b+c=0\) we get \(a+c=2b\), so
\(s=\dfrac{a+b+c}{2}=\dfrac{2b+b}{2}=\dfrac{3b}{2}\), and \(s-b=\dfrac{3b}{2}-b=\dfrac{b}{2}\).

Now use the half-angle formulas \(\tan\dfrac{A}{2}=\sqrt{\dfrac{(s-b)(s-c)}{s(s-a)}}\) and \(\tan\dfrac{C}{2}=\sqrt{\dfrac{(s-a)(s-b)}{s(s-c)}}\). Taking reciprocals,
\(\cot\dfrac{A}{2}=\sqrt{\dfrac{s(s-a)}{(s-b)(s-c)}}\) and \(\cot\dfrac{C}{2}=\sqrt{\dfrac{s(s-c)}{(s-a)(s-b)}}\).

Multiply the two, and the factors \((s-a)\) and \((s-c)\) cancel between numerator and denominator:
\(\cot\dfrac{A}{2}\cot\dfrac{C}{2}=\sqrt{\dfrac{s(s-a)}{(s-b)(s-c)}\cdot\dfrac{s(s-c)}{(s-a)(s-b)}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{s^{2}(s-a)(s-c)}{(s-a)(s-c)(s-b)^{2}}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{s^{2}}{(s-b)^{2}}}=\dfrac{s}{s-b}\).

Substituting the two values found above:
\(\cot\dfrac{A}{2}\cot\dfrac{C}{2}=\dfrac{3b/2}{b/2}=3\).

Hence (B).

why: The old solution named a column operation that does not produce the claimed structure, said 'Vandermonde-like', and then asserted the answer without expanding or fixing the sign.
solution:
Observe that every row sums to 1: \((1-\alpha)+(\alpha-\alpha^{2})+\alpha^{2}=1\), and likewise for the \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\) rows.

Step 1 — apply \(C_1\to C_1+C_2+C_3\) (this leaves the determinant unchanged). Every entry of the first column becomes 1:
\(\begin{vmatrix}1 & \alpha-\alpha^{2} & \alpha^{2}\\ 1 & \beta-\beta^{2} & \beta^{2}\\ 1 & \gamma-\gamma^{2} & \gamma^{2}\end{vmatrix}\)

Step 2 — apply \(C_2\to C_2+C_3\). The second column becomes \(\alpha-\alpha^{2}+\alpha^{2}=\alpha\), and similarly \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\):
\(\begin{vmatrix}1 & \alpha & \alpha^{2}\\ 1 & \beta & \beta^{2}\\ 1 & \gamma & \gamma^{2}\end{vmatrix}\)

Step 3 — expand this Vandermonde determinant. Do \(R_2\to R_2-R_1\) and \(R_3\to R_3-R_1\):
\(\begin{vmatrix}1 & \alpha & \alpha^{2}\\ 0 & \beta-\alpha & \beta^{2}-\alpha^{2}\\ 0 & \gamma-\alpha & \gamma^{2}-\alpha^{2}\end{vmatrix}\)
Expanding along the first column and factoring \((\beta-\alpha)\) out of \(R_2\) and \((\gamma-\alpha)\) out of \(R_3\), using \(\beta^{2}-\alpha^{2}=(\beta-\alpha)(\beta+\alpha)\):
\(=(\beta-\alpha)(\gamma-\alpha)\begin{vmatrix}1 & \beta+\alpha\\ 1 & \gamma+\alpha\end{vmatrix}=(\beta-\alpha)(\gamma-\alpha)\big[(\gamma+\alpha)-(\beta+\alpha)\big]=(\beta-\alpha)(\gamma-\alpha)(\gamma-\beta)\).

Step 4 — match the option form. Flip the sign of two factors: \((\beta-\alpha)=-(\alpha-\beta)\) and \((\gamma-\beta)=-(\beta-\gamma)\). The two minus signs cancel:
\((\beta-\alpha)(\gamma-\alpha)(\gamma-\beta)=(-1)(\alpha-\beta)\cdot(\gamma-\alpha)\cdot(-1)(\beta-\gamma)=(\alpha-\beta)(\beta-\gamma)(\gamma-\alpha)\).

Hence (B).

why: The inequality argument was sound, but it was framed as adopting whichever reading of the stem makes the paper's answer come out right; the ordering in fact needs only 0<P(A)<P(B)<1, so the ratio never enters.
solution:
Write \(p=P(A\cap B)\). The three quantities being compared are
\(P(A\cap B)=p\), \(\quad P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{p}{P(B)}\), \(\quad P(B\mid A)=\dfrac{p}{P(A)}\),
all with the same numerator \(p\), so the ordering is decided entirely by the denominators. Take \(p>0\); if \(p=0\) all three are 0 and no strict ordering exists.

First comparison. Since \(0<P(B)<1\), dividing the positive number \(p\) by \(P(B)\) enlarges it:
\(P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{p}{P(B)}>\dfrac{p}{1}=p=P(A\cap B)\).

Second comparison. Since \(0<P(A)<P(B)\), taking reciprocals of positive numbers reverses the inequality: \(\dfrac{1}{P(A)}>\dfrac{1}{P(B)}\). Multiplying through by \(p>0\):
\(P(B\mid A)=\dfrac{p}{P(A)}>\dfrac{p}{P(B)}=P(A\mid B)\).

Chaining the two:
\(P(A\cap B)<P(A\mid B)<P(B\mid A)\).

[Note: only \(0<P(A)<P(B)<1\) was used. The stem's ratio condition \(2P(A)=3P(B)\) would give \(P(A)=\tfrac{3}{2}P(B)>P(B)\), which conflicts with \(P(A)<P(B)\); since the ratio plays no part in either comparison above, the ordering is unaffected either way.]

Hence (D).

why: The old solution hid the squaring algebra behind 'Squaring and simplifying gives'; the half-angle route below avoids squaring altogether, so no extraneous roots are created in the first place.
solution:
Use \(1+\cos x=2\cos^{2}\dfrac{x}{2}\) and \(\sin x=2\sin\dfrac{x}{2}\cos\dfrac{x}{2}\):
\(\csc x+\cot x=\dfrac{1}{\sin x}+\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}=\dfrac{1+\cos x}{\sin x}=\dfrac{2\cos^{2}\frac{x}{2}}{2\sin\frac{x}{2}\cos\frac{x}{2}}=\dfrac{\cos\frac{x}{2}}{\sin\frac{x}{2}}=\cot\dfrac{x}{2}\).
This is valid wherever \(\sin x\neq 0\), which the original equation already requires.

So the equation becomes \(\cot\dfrac{x}{2}=\sqrt{3}\).

For \(0<x<2\pi\) we have \(0<\dfrac{x}{2}<\pi\), and \(\cot\) is strictly decreasing on \((0,\pi)\), so it attains the value \(\sqrt{3}\) exactly once there. Since \(\cot\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\sqrt{3}\), that point is \(\dfrac{x}{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\), i.e. \(x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\).

Substituting back: \(\csc\dfrac{\pi}{3}+\cot\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{3}}=\sqrt{3}\), so it satisfies the equation.

The other listed values fail: at \(x=\pi\), \(\sin x=0\), so \(\csc x\) and \(\cot x\) are undefined; at \(x=\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\), \(\csc x=-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\) and \(\cot x=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), whose sum is \(-\sqrt{3}\neq\sqrt{3}\).

Hence (B).

why: The old solution wrote down the discriminant of g and then tagged '(can be shown)' onto the one claim the whole question turns on — that it is negative — without expanding it.
solution:
Let \(f(x)=ax^{2}+bx+c\). For \(f\) to be positive for every real \(x\) it must open upwards and never meet the axis, so
\(a>0\) and \(b^{2}-4ac<0\).

Differentiate: \(f'(x)=2ax+b\) and \(f''(x)=2a\). Therefore
\(g(x)=(ax^{2}+bx+c)+(2ax+b)+2a=ax^{2}+(b+2a)x+(c+b+2a)\),
again a quadratic, with the same leading coefficient \(a>0\).

Now expand its discriminant term by term:
\((b+2a)^{2}-4a(c+b+2a)=b^{2}+4ab+4a^{2}-4ac-4ab-8a^{2}\).
The \(4ab\) terms cancel and \(4a^{2}-8a^{2}=-4a^{2}\), leaving
\(=b^{2}-4ac-4a^{2}=(b^{2}-4ac)-4a^{2}\).

Both pieces are negative: \(b^{2}-4ac<0\) by hypothesis, and \(-4a^{2}<0\) because \(a\neq 0\). So the discriminant of \(g\) is strictly negative.

A quadratic with positive leading coefficient and negative discriminant has no real zero, so it never changes sign and never reaches 0; its sign is that of its leading coefficient. Hence \(g(x)>0\) for every real \(x\) — strictly, so the weaker option \(g(x)\geq 0\) is not the sharpest true statement.

Hence (B).

why: The old solution reached the condition b^2/(ac)=q^2/(pr) and then jumped straight to the answer with '(can be shown via the ratio condition)', skipping the cancellation that is the entire point.
solution:
Let the roots of \(ax^{2}+bx+c=0\) be \(\alpha,\beta\) in the ratio \(k:1\), and the roots of \(px^{2}+qx+r=0\) be \(\gamma,\delta\) in the same ratio \(k:1\).

Step 1 — turn the ratio into a coefficient relation. For the first equation \(\alpha+\beta=-\dfrac{b}{a}\) and \(\alpha\beta=\dfrac{c}{a}\), so
\(\dfrac{(\alpha+\beta)^{2}}{\alpha\beta}=\dfrac{b^{2}/a^{2}}{c/a}=\dfrac{b^{2}}{ac}\).
Writing the roots as \(\alpha=kt,\ \beta=t\), the same expression is
\(\dfrac{(kt+t)^{2}}{kt\cdot t}=\dfrac{t^{2}(k+1)^{2}}{kt^{2}}=\dfrac{(k+1)^{2}}{k}\).
So \(\dfrac{b^{2}}{ac}=\dfrac{(k+1)^{2}}{k}\), and by the identical argument \(\dfrac{q^{2}}{pr}=\dfrac{(k+1)^{2}}{k}\).

Step 2 — call this common value \(m\), so \(ac=\dfrac{b^{2}}{m}\) and \(pr=\dfrac{q^{2}}{m}\). Substitute into the discriminants:
\(D_{1}=b^{2}-4ac=b^{2}-\dfrac{4b^{2}}{m}=b^{2}\cdot\dfrac{m-4}{m}\),
\(D_{2}=q^{2}-4pr=q^{2}-\dfrac{4q^{2}}{m}=q^{2}\cdot\dfrac{m-4}{m}\).

Step 3 — divide. The factor \(\dfrac{m-4}{m}\) is the same in both and cancels (it is non-zero precisely when \(D_{2}\neq 0\), i.e. \(k\neq 1\), which the division requires anyway):
\(\dfrac{D_{1}}{D_{2}}=\dfrac{b^{2}\cdot\frac{m-4}{m}}{q^{2}\cdot\frac{m-4}{m}}=\dfrac{b^{2}}{q^{2}}\).

Hence (B).

why: The old solution named the reversal law and gestured at one product without associating the factors, and never said why uniqueness of the inverse lets you conclude from it.
solution:
Since \(A\) and \(B\) are invertible, \(A^{-1}\) and \(B^{-1}\) exist. Multiply \(AB\) by the candidate \(B^{-1}A^{-1}\) on each side, regrouping by associativity:

\((AB)(B^{-1}A^{-1})=A(BB^{-1})A^{-1}=A\,I\,A^{-1}=AA^{-1}=I\),

\((B^{-1}A^{-1})(AB)=B^{-1}(A^{-1}A)B=B^{-1}\,I\,B=B^{-1}B=I\).

So \(B^{-1}A^{-1}\) is a two-sided inverse of \(AB\). The inverse of a matrix is unique, therefore \((AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}\).

The order cannot be swapped: \((AB)(A^{-1}B^{-1})=A(BA^{-1})B^{-1}\), and \(BA^{-1}\) does not collapse to \(I\) unless \(A\) and \(B\) happen to commute.

Hence (A).

why: The old solution quoted A·adj(A)=det(A)I as a bare result with no reason; the cofactor-expansion argument for it is two lines and belongs in the answer.
solution:
Let \(A=[a_{ij}]\) be of order \(n\) and let \(C_{ij}\) denote the cofactor of \(a_{ij}\). By definition the adjoint is the transpose of the cofactor matrix, so \(B=\mathrm{adj}(A)\) has \((i,j)\) entry \(C_{ji}\).

The \((i,j)\) entry of \(AB\) is therefore
\((AB)_{ij}=\sum_{t=1}^{n}a_{it}\,C_{jt}\).

Diagonal entries \((i=j)\): \(\sum_{t}a_{it}C_{it}\) is exactly the cofactor expansion of \(\det A\) along row \(i\), so \((AB)_{ii}=\det A=k\).

Off-diagonal entries \((i\neq j)\): \(\sum_{t}a_{it}C_{jt}\) is the cofactor expansion along row \(j\) of the matrix obtained from \(A\) by replacing row \(j\) with a copy of row \(i\) — the cofactors \(C_{jt}\) do not involve row \(j\), so they are unchanged by that replacement. That matrix has two identical rows (rows \(i\) and \(j\)), so its determinant is 0, giving \((AB)_{ij}=0\).

So \(AB\) carries \(k\) all along its diagonal and 0 everywhere else, that is \(AB=kI\), written \(kl\) in the options.

Hence (B).

why: The old solution asserted a formula for cos(alpha-beta) carrying an unexplained square root of ambiguous sign, then hid the whole cancellation behind 'substituting and simplifying gives'.
solution:
Put \(u=\theta-\alpha\) and \(v=\theta-\beta\), so that \(\cos u=a\) and \(\cos v=b\). Then
\(\alpha-\beta=(\theta-\beta)-(\theta-\alpha)=v-u\).

Step 1 — expand the cosine of the difference:
\(\cos(\alpha-\beta)=\cos(v-u)=\cos v\cos u+\sin v\sin u=ab+s\), where \(s=\sin u\sin v\).

Step 2 — record what \(s^{2}\) is (its sign is never needed):
\(s^{2}=\sin^{2}u\,\sin^{2}v=(1-\cos^{2}u)(1-\cos^{2}v)=(1-a^{2})(1-b^{2})=1-a^{2}-b^{2}+a^{2}b^{2}\).

Step 3 — write \(c=\cos(\alpha-\beta)=ab+s\), so \(\sin^{2}(\alpha-\beta)=1-c^{2}\), and expand the required expression:
\(\sin^{2}(\alpha-\beta)+2ab\cos(\alpha-\beta)=1-c^{2}+2abc\)
\(=1-(ab+s)^{2}+2ab(ab+s)\)
\(=1-\big(a^{2}b^{2}+2abs+s^{2}\big)+2a^{2}b^{2}+2abs\).
The terms \(-2abs\) and \(+2abs\) cancel, and \(-a^{2}b^{2}+2a^{2}b^{2}=a^{2}b^{2}\), leaving
\(=1+a^{2}b^{2}-s^{2}\).

Step 4 — substitute \(s^{2}\) from Step 2:
\(=1+a^{2}b^{2}-\big(1-a^{2}-b^{2}+a^{2}b^{2}\big)=1+a^{2}b^{2}-1+a^{2}+b^{2}-a^{2}b^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}\).

Only \(s^{2}\) ever appears, so the unknown sign of \(\sin u\sin v\) does not affect the answer.

Hence (A).

why: The old solution described a rotation it never carried out, produced a garbled half-computed coordinate pair, and then trailed off into asserting the answer.
solution:
Let \(P=(-1,-1)\) and \(Q=(-\sqrt{3},\sqrt{3})\).

Step 1 — find the side length. 
\(PQ^{2}=(-\sqrt{3}+1)^{2}+(\sqrt{3}+1)^{2}=(3-2\sqrt{3}+1)+(3+2\sqrt{3}+1)=(4-2\sqrt{3})+(4+2\sqrt{3})=8\),
so \(PQ=2\sqrt{2}\).

Step 2 — the third vertex \(R\) must satisfy \(RP^{2}=RQ^{2}=8\). Compute \(RP^{2}\) for each option:

\((-\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2})\): \(RP^{2}=(-\sqrt{2}+1)^{2}+(\sqrt{2}+1)^{2}=(3-2\sqrt{2})+(3+2\sqrt{2})=6\neq 8\).

\((\sqrt{2},-\sqrt{2})\): \(RP^{2}=(\sqrt{2}+1)^{2}+(-\sqrt{2}+1)^{2}=(3+2\sqrt{2})+(3-2\sqrt{2})=6\neq 8\).

\((1,-1)\): \(RP^{2}=(1+1)^{2}+(-1+1)^{2}=4+0=4\neq 8\).

\((1,1)\): \(RP^{2}=(1+1)^{2}+(1+1)^{2}=4+4=8\) — this one survives.

Step 3 — confirm the surviving point against \(Q\) as well:
\(RQ^{2}=(1+\sqrt{3})^{2}+(1-\sqrt{3})^{2}=(1+2\sqrt{3}+3)+(1-2\sqrt{3}+3)=(4+2\sqrt{3})+(4-2\sqrt{3})=8\).

So for \(R=(1,1)\), \(RP=RQ=PQ=2\sqrt{2}\): all three sides are equal and the triangle is equilateral. (An equilateral triangle on \(PQ\) has two possible third vertices, one on each side of \(PQ\); the question asks only where the third vertex may lie, so exhibiting this one settles it.)

Hence (C).

why: The old solution reached for cube roots of unity and cited a numerical check as its justification; the answer follows directly from the equation itself in two lines.
solution:
Expand the equation: \(x(x+1)+1=x^{2}+x+1=0\).

Since \(k\) is a root, \(k^{2}+k+1=0\), which rearranges to
\(k^{2}=-(k+1)\).

The sum of the two roots of \(x^{2}+x+1=0\) is \(-\dfrac{1}{1}=-1\), so if one root is \(k\) the other is
\(-1-k=-(k+1)\).

Comparing the two displayed lines, the other root \(-(k+1)\) is precisely \(k^{2}\).

A cross-check with the product of roots: the product is \(\dfrac{1}{1}=1\), and \(k\cdot k^{2}=k^{3}\); multiplying \(k^{2}+k+1=0\) by \((k-1)\) gives \(k^{3}-1=0\), so \(k^{3}=1\), as required. Note also \(k\neq 0\), since \(0^{2}+0+1=1\neq 0\), so \(k\) and \(k^{2}\) are genuinely the two roots.

Hence (C).

why: The old solution set up the discriminant correctly but replaced the expansion and the recognition of the perfect square with 'Expanding and simplifying gives'.
solution:
Collect the \(x\) terms:
\(x^{2}-ax-bx-cx+bc+ca=x^{2}-(a+b+c)x+(bc+ca)=0\).

Equal roots means the discriminant is zero:
\((a+b+c)^{2}-4(bc+ca)=0\).

Expand \((a+b+c)^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+2ab+2bc+2ca\) and subtract \(4bc+4ca\):
\(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+2ab+2bc+2ca-4bc-4ca=a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+2ab-2bc-2ca\).

This is a perfect square. Expanding \((a+b-c)^{2}\) gives
\(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+2ab-2ac-2bc\),
which matches the previous line term for term.

So the condition is \((a+b-c)^{2}=0\), and since a square vanishes only when its base does,
\(a+b-c=0\).

Hence (C).
